sections.model_projection: The model projects Seattle to win 26.48 to 17.84, a margin of 8.63 points in favor of the Seahawks. The market spread sits at Arizona +10.0, meaning the model is about 1.4 points more favorable to the Cardinals than the current line. The projected total of 44.32 is nearly identical to the market total of 44.5. Seattle's win probability is 80.3% per the model.
sections.offensive_matchup: Seattle's offense (ranked 2nd in points per game at 29.2, 5th in offensive success rate at 47.7%) runs into an Arizona defense that ranks 24th in defensive EPA per play — a measure of how many expected points a defense surrenders on each snap — and 27th in defensive success rate at 47.6%. Arizona's pass defense is a particular liability, ranking 25th in defensive passing EPA per play at +0.145, while Seattle's passing attack generates a positive 0.164 EPA per pass play (7th). On the other side, Arizona's offense ranks 22nd in scoring at 20.9 points per game and 18th in offensive EPA per play, facing a Seattle defense that ranks 2nd overall in defensive EPA per play at -0.116. The structural mismatch strongly favors Seattle moving the ball and limiting Arizona's production.
sections.quarterback_edge: Insufficient reliable data on current season performance for both quarterbacks, as neither has recorded season attempts yet. Based on career metrics available in the package, Sam Darnold (Seattle) carries a career EPA per dropback of +0.017 and a career yards per attempt of 7.61 across 58 games, while Jacoby Brissett (Arizona) shows a career EPA per dropback of -0.029 and 6.58 yards per attempt across 37 games. The model assigns Seattle a slight edge at this position, worth roughly 0.24 points. Both starters are flagged as returning starters with moderate confidence.
sections.trenches: The offensive line matchup is one of the sharpest edges in this game. Arizona's offensive line ranks 30th in line yards (yards credited to the line per rush, at 2.53) and 24th in sack rate allowed (7.9% of dropbacks), while Seattle's defensive front generates pressure on 27.5% of dropbacks (6th) and surrenders just 2.56 line yards per rush (1st). Seattle's own offensive line ranks 25th in line yards at 2.72, but it faces an Arizona defensive front that ranks 28th in pressure rate at 18.7% and 22nd in rush defense EPA per play. The net result is that Seattle's run defense dominates Arizona's run game, while Arizona's pass rush offers little resistance to Seattle's passing attack — the offensive line edge is worth nearly a full point to Seattle.
sections.explosive_play_edge: Seattle generates explosive plays — defined as rushes of 10-plus yards or passes of 20-plus yards — on 9.5% of plays (10th), while Arizona allows them on 10.6% of plays (29th), the second-worst rate in the league. Conversely, Seattle limits opponent explosive plays to just 6.6% (2nd best), while Arizona produces them on only 7.2% of plays (28th). This creates a one-sided dynamic: Seattle has a realistic path to chunk plays downfield, while Arizona is unlikely to generate the big gains needed to keep pace. The explosive play edge is rated at maximum in Seattle's favor.
sections.third_down_red_zone: Seattle's third-down defense is the best in the league, holding opponents to a 32.8% conversion rate, while Arizona converts third downs at a 45.3% clip allowed (29th) — meaning Seattle's offense should sustain drives while Arizona's offense will struggle to extend them. In the red zone, Seattle scores touchdowns on 62.9% of trips (14th) and earns 3.37 points per scoring opportunity (5th), compared to Arizona's defense allowing touchdowns on 59.6% of red-zone visits (18th). Arizona's offense converts red-zone trips to touchdowns at just a 50.0% rate (26th), and earns only 2.63 points per scoring opportunity (25th), facing a Seattle defense that allows touchdowns on just 47.6% of red-zone trips (2nd). The compounding effect of Seattle winning both the third-down and red-zone battles is a significant scoring margin driver.
sections.roster_talent: Insufficient reliable data on talent ratings for both rosters, as the talent field is not modeled for NFL teams in this package. Seattle does hold a meaningful edge in roster continuity (0.94 vs. Arizona's 0.85) and returning production (89% total vs. 70%), including 100% returning passing production and 91% receiving production versus Arizona's 75% and 79% respectively. Arizona's offensive line has logged only 53 returning starts compared to Seattle's 85, a concrete indicator of less experienced line continuity heading into the season. These continuity advantages contribute a small but real edge to Seattle in the model.
sections.recent_form: Insufficient reliable data on recent form trends, as both teams have zero games played in the current season and no form shift is recorded for either side. The model assigns a neutral recent form edge with zero points impact in either direction. All metrics in this package carry a low-sample flag reflecting preseason or prior-season blended data.
sections.market_movement: The spread has held at Arizona +10.0 since the first market snapshot on DraftKings, with zero movement across 51 snapshots on five books. The total has similarly remained static at 44.5 with no movement recorded. There is no book disagreement on the spread. Public ticket and money percentages are unavailable, so no conclusions about betting flow can be drawn. The market and model are closely aligned, with the model projecting a margin 1.4 points tighter than the current line.

sections.expected_game_script: Seattle figures to control the line of scrimmage defensively from the opening series, limiting Arizona's run game — which ranks 26th in rushing EPA per play at -0.125 — and forcing Brissett into a pass-heavy approach against a Seattle secondary that ranks 8th in defensive passing EPA per play. Arizona already leans heavily pass (66.4% neutral-script pass rate, 1st in the league), so the game script should accelerate that tendency as the Cardinals fall behind. Seattle's offense, running the league's lowest neutral-script pass rate at 53.4% (31st), will likely try to establish the run early, though their offensive line's 25th-ranked line yards figure may limit that avenue against an Arizona front that is at least average against the run. If Seattle's passing attack — generating 0.164 EPA per pass play — can exploit Arizona's 25th-ranked pass defense, the Seahawks can build a lead that forces Arizona into obvious passing situations. Arizona's best hope is converting third downs at their 42.0% offensive rate and using play-action (29.8% rate, 4th) to generate chunk plays against a Seattle defense that otherwise limits explosives. The model sees this as a double-digit Seattle win with the Cardinals unable to generate enough sustained offense to keep pace, though Arizona's home field and pass-heavy identity give them a narrow path if they win the turnover battle.
